title: Set a row of tiles with 3 mm joints
instruction: Lay the four tiles in one row along the straightedge, each tile square to it and against it, with a 3 mm joint between neighbouring tiles.
context: Tile setters lay the first course of a floor along a straightedge and keep every joint the same width, squaring each tile as it comes out of the box any way round; a millimetre of drift per tile adds up across a room and shows in every row after it. Done by: tile and stone setters.
setup: A dark grey aluminium straightedge (30 cm long, 1.2 cm wide, 5 mm tall) is fixed to the table, running straight out from the arms 22 cm left of centre, from 12 to 42 cm in front of the arm bases. Four blue glazed porcelain tiles (6 x 6 cm, 2 cm thick, 170 g each) lie flat on the table in a line on the straightedge's left side, 30 cm left of centre, their centres 15, 23, 31 and 39 cm in front of the arm bases, turned from square to the table edge by 25, 10, 30 and 15 degrees in that order (anticlockwise seen from above). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: A tile is set when, at the end, it lies flat on the table (tilted at most 2 degrees), is square to the straightedge (turned at most 2 degrees), touches the straightedge or is at most 1 mm from it, lies within the straightedge's length, and is still (moving under 1 cm/s). Each set tile scores 0.1. Each joint between two neighbouring set tiles in the row scores 0.2 if it is 2 to 4 mm wide at its narrowest point; the row is the set tiles on the side of the straightedge with the most of them, so tiles set on the other side earn 0.1 each but nothing for their joints. All four tiles set in one row with three good joints: 1.0. If any tile ends face down (tilted more than 135 degrees) or off the table, the score is 0; a tile on its edge is only not set.
reset_notes: Lay the four tiles back in their starting line on the straightedge's left side, centres 15, 23, 31 and 39 cm out, turned 25, 10, 30 and 15 degrees anticlockwise from square in that order (a protractor or a printed template sets the angles).
fidelity: Real tiles are bedded in mortar and levelled; these lie dry on a hard table. They are 6 cm squares at a real 2 cm paver thickness, scaled down from 30-60 cm tiles so the gripper can span them, and no spacers are provided. The straightedge is a fixed 5 mm strip. Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than porcelain on a floor, so a tile won't slide into place the way it would on wet mortar.
